**Jacek Karpiński** (1927–2010) was a Polish computer engineer and inventor born in Turin, Italy, into a family of intellectuals and mountaineers. During World War II, he joined the Polish underground resistance, sustaining severe injuries but continuing to fight and participate in the Warsaw Uprising. After the war, he rapidly advanced academically, graduating from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951 and undertaking pioneering projects in computing in Poland.
Karpiński designed several innovative computing devices, including the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH, 1957), the transistor-based differential equations analyzer AKAT-1 (1959), one of the world's first perceptrons (1964), the KAR-65 computer (1968), and the highly advanced K-202 minicomputer (early 1970s), notable for its asynchronic architecture, floating-point representation, memory segmentation with paging, and high operation speed. Despite significant technological innovations, his projects faced political and institutional opposition, leading to limited production and recognition. He spent part of his later life abroad before returning to Poland, where he advised on computer science and pursued business ventures. Posthumously, Karpiński was honored for his contributions and remains a controversial yet highly regarded figure in the history of Polish computing.
